title: Cardiovascular Comprehensive Set 1: Myocardial Mechanics (Short answer)

questions.prompt: What is the name of the basic contractile unit of the myocardial cell, which is delineated by Z disks?
questions.modelAnswer: The sarcomere.

questions.prompt: Which specific subunit of the troponin complex is responsible for binding calcium to initiate the removal of tropomyosin's inhibition of the actin-myosin interaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Troponin C.

questions.prompt: The "thick filament" of cardiac muscle is primarily composed of which protein, and what site does its globular heads contain and what enzymatic activity does it have?
questions.modelAnswer: Myosin; the heads contain actin-binding sites and myosin ATPase activity.

questions.prompt: In terms of myocardial tissue behavior, what is the functional purpose of the gap junctions located at the intercalated disks?
questions.modelAnswer: They provide low-resistance pathways for the rapid spread of action potentials, allowing the heart to act as an electrical syncytium.

questions.prompt: What is the specific physiological role of the transverse (T) tubules during the electrical activation of a cardiac muscle cell?
questions.modelAnswer: They carry the depolarization from the sarcolemmal membrane to the cell interior.

questions.prompt: Explain the concept of "calcium-induced calcium release" (CICR) as it occurs during the plateau of the cardiac action potential.
questions.modelAnswer: The entry of trigger calcium through L-type channels during the plateau stimulates the ryanodine receptors to release a much larger amount of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.prompt: Which membrane protein is responsible for the entry of "trigger calcium" from the extracellular fluid during the action potential?
questions.modelAnswer: L-type calcium channels (also called dihydropyridine receptors).

questions.prompt: How does the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) maintain a low internal free calcium concentration despite the presence of high total calcium stores?
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium is bound to calsequestrin, a low-affinity, high-capacity binding protein.

questions.prompt: By what primary mechanism is calcium reaccumulated into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to allow for myocardial relaxation?
questions.modelAnswer: The SERCA pump (Sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca^(2+) ATPase).

questions.prompt: Describe the effect of phospholamban phosphorylation on the speed of cardiac relaxation.
questions.modelAnswer: Phosphorylation of phospholamban disinhibits the SERCA pump, resulting in a faster rate of calcium uptake and faster relaxation.

questions.prompt: Define myocardial contractility (inotropism) and identify the primary intracellular factor that determines its magnitude.
questions.modelAnswer: Contractility is the intrinsic ability to develop force at a given muscle length; it is determined by the intracellular calcium concentration.

questions.prompt: How does an increase in heart rate (the Bowditch staircase) result in increased tension development on a cellular level?
questions.modelAnswer: A higher frequency of action potentials increases the total influx of trigger calcium and increases the amount of calcium stored and released by the SR.

questions.prompt: Explain the molecular mechanism by which cardiac glycosides, such as digoxin, produce a positive inotropic effect.
questions.modelAnswer: They inhibit Na^+/K^+ ATPase, which increases intracellular [Na^+]; this reduces the gradient for the Na^+-Ca^(2+) exchanger, leading to an increase in intracellular [Ca^(2+)].

questions.prompt: Define "preload" in the context of ventricular function and identify the parameter most commonly used to approximate it in a clinical setting.
questions.modelAnswer: Preload is the resting length from which the muscle contracts; it is approximated by left ventricular end-diastolic volume.

questions.prompt: How is the "afterload" for the left ventricle defined in terms of systemic hemodynamics?
questions.modelAnswer: Aortic pressure (or mean arterial pressure).

questions.prompt: State the formula for the ejection fraction and identify its normal resting value in a healthy adult.
questions.modelAnswer: Ejection Fraction = Stroke Volume / End-Diastolic Volume; normal is approximately 0.55 (55%).

questions.prompt: According to the Frank-Starling Law of the heart, what is the relationship between ventricular end-diastolic volume and the volume ejected during systole?
questions.modelAnswer: The volume of blood ejected (stroke volume) is determined by the volume present at the end of diastole.

questions.prompt: Apart from filament overlap, what are the two additional length-dependent mechanisms that increase the force of contraction when a cardiac muscle fiber is stretched?
questions.modelAnswer: (1) Increased calcium sensitivity of troponin C; (2) Increased calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.prompt: Describe the two ionic mechanisms by which acetylcholine (parasympathetic stimulation) reduces the contractility of atrial muscle.
questions.modelAnswer: (1) It decreases inward calcium current during the plateau; (2) It increases the outward K^+ current (I_(K-ACh)), which shortens the action potential duration.

questions.prompt: Why does cardiac muscle normally operate only on the ascending limb of its length-tension curve, unlike skeletal muscle?
questions.modelAnswer: Cardiac muscle has high resting tension and stiffness, which prevents stretching the fibers beyond their optimal length (L_(max)).
